title: Etosha vs Okavango: Waterhole Drives in Namibia or Mokoro Channels in Botswana?
meta_title: Etosha vs Okavango: Wildlife, Costs and Seasons Compared
meta_description: Etosha vs Okavango compared: wildlife, best months, daily costs and the route between them, so you can choose one or combine both. Ask our team.
excerpt: Etosha vs Okavango: Namibia's waterhole park against Botswana's wetland delta, compared on wildlife, seasons, costs and how to combine them in one trip.
content:
Etosha vs Okavango comes down to how you like to watch animals. Etosha in northern Namibia is a dry park where wildlife walks in to drink at waterholes and you can drive yourself, while Botswana's Okavango Delta is a seasonal wetland you explore by mokoro, boat and on foot from remote, mostly fly-in camps.

Both sit near the top of most southern Africa wish lists, yet they cost very different amounts, peak in slightly different months and need different logistics. This Etosha vs Okavango guide compares the wildlife, a typical safari day, the seasons, realistic costs and the route between them, so you can pick one, or plan both, with your eyes open.

Photo by m_oros on Unsplash

Quick Facts

  • Etosha: 22,270 km² national park in northern Namibia, built around a salt pan of about 4,760 km²
  • Okavango Delta: Inland delta in north-west Botswana, fed by rain that falls in Angola and arrives months later
  • Best months: Etosha May to October; Okavango June to October, when the flood is high and the bush is dry
  • Park fees: Etosha N$280 per non-SADC adult plus N$60 per car; Moremi BWP 270 per adult per day (both checked November 2026)
  • Getting in: Etosha by road from Windhoek (Halali camp is about 451 km); most Delta camps by light aircraft from Maun
  • Etosha vs Okavango verdict: Etosha suits self-drivers, families and mid-range budgets; the Okavango suits water safaris, walking and privacy

Etosha vs Okavango: What Is the Real Difference?

The real difference in the Etosha vs Okavango question is water. Etosha is semi-arid, so animals are pulled to fixed waterholes and you wait for them; the Okavango Delta is a maze of channels, lagoons and islands, so you move through the habitat by boat or on foot.

Etosha feels open, with the white pan on the horizon and mostly gravel roads. The three main Namibia Wildlife Resorts camps inside the park, Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni, each have a floodlit waterhole you can watch after dark.

The Okavango works the other way round. Much of the Delta is split into private concessions with few camps, so you may not see another vehicle all day, while Moremi Game Reserve on the eastern side takes self-drive 4x4s and budget mobile safaris. Our Okavango Delta vs Chobe comparison explains how the Delta fits with the rest of northern Botswana.

Which Has Better Wildlife, Etosha or the Okavango Delta?

Neither is simply better: Etosha gives easier, more predictable sightings in the dry season, including black rhino, while the Okavango offers a wider mix of habitats, all of the Big Five, and water species such as hippo, red lechwe and sitatunga that Etosha does not have.

Photo by Ria Truter on Unsplash

Wildlife in Etosha

Etosha is home to about 114 mammal species. Elephant, lion, giraffe, zebra, springbok and gemsbok are everyday sights at the waterholes from June, and black rhino often drink after dark at the floodlit camp waterholes. Leopard and cheetah are present but harder to find. There are no buffalo or hippo, so Etosha cannot give you the full Big Five.

Wildlife in the Okavango Delta

The Okavango Delta holds big herds of elephant and buffalo, lion prides that hunt across the floodplains, leopard in the woodland, and some of the best chances in Africa of seeing African wild dog, especially around Moremi and the neighbouring concessions. Hippo and crocodile fill the channels. Rhino have been reintroduced, but sightings are rare.

For a first-timer who wants a high count of animals with little effort, the Etosha vs Okavango verdict tilts slightly to Etosha in the dry months. For variety, predators and atmosphere, the Delta usually wins, which is also why it costs more.

How Does a Day on Safari Differ?

On an Etosha vs Okavango day, the contrast is sharp. A day in Etosha is spent in a vehicle moving between waterholes, with strict gate times from sunrise to sunset. A day in the Okavango mixes game drives with mokoro trips, motorboat cruises and guided walks, and private concessions often add night drives.

Photo by Colin Watts on Unsplash

In Etosha you cannot leave the roads or walk, but the waterhole rhythm is relaxed: choose a waterhole, switch off the engine and let the animals come. Our Etosha safari planning guide covers the camps, gates and nights for each part of the park.

In the Delta, days run from a dawn activity to a long lunch and an afternoon outing into sundowners. What you do depends on the water level at your camp: a water camp leans on mokoro and boat trips, a land camp on game drives.

When Is the Best Time for Etosha and the Okavango?

The best overlap for Etosha vs Okavango is June to October. Etosha is at its best from May to October when the bush is dry and animals crowd the waterholes, and the Okavango flood is high from about June to August, with the strongest game viewing as the land dries into September and October.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

The Delta's flood timing surprises many travellers. Rain falls in the Angolan highlands in the southern summer and takes around four months to arrive, so the Delta is fullest in Botswana's dry winter, usually peaking around July or August.

MonthsEtoshaOkavango Delta
January to MarchGreen season, hot with afternoon storms; animals spread out, good birdingWet season; lush and quiet, water levels low before the flood arrives
April to MayRains ending, cooler; game starts returning to waterholesFlood arriving; mokoro trips become possible in more areas
June to AugustPeak dry season, cold mornings, excellent waterhole sightingsFlood at its highest, the classic time for water activities
September to OctoberHot and very dry, the strongest concentrations of the yearWater receding, superb predator viewing, high season prices
November to DecemberFirst rains; game disperses, fewer visitorsHot, rains begin; low-season rates in many camps

For month-by-month detail on each country, read our guides to the best time to visit Namibia and the best time to visit Botswana.

How Much Does an Etosha vs Okavango Safari Cost?

In any Etosha vs Okavango cost comparison, Etosha is cheaper by a wide margin. Park fees are modest and there is a full range of lodges inside and just outside the gates, while most Okavango camps sit in private concessions reached by light aircraft, which pushes the daily cost much higher.

Etosha's entry fee for international (non-SADC) adults is N$280 per person, made up of a park fee and a conservation fee, plus N$60 for a car with up to 10 seats, under the Namibian Government Gazette fee schedule in force from 1 April 2026 (checked November 2026). In Botswana, Moremi Game Reserve charges BWP 270 per international adult per day (checked November 2026). Private concession camps include their own conservation fees in their rates. Fees change, so confirm them before you book.

StyleEtoshaOkavango Delta
BudgetAbout USD 200 to 350 per day on a guided camping or simple lodge tourAbout USD 250 to 450 per day on a mokoro camping trip from Maun
Mid-rangeAbout USD 350 to 600 per day with lodges near the gatesAbout USD 500 to 900 per day in Moremi or Khwai lodges and mobile camps
LuxuryAbout USD 600 to 1,200 per day in private reserves next to the parkAbout USD 1,200 to 3,000 or more per day in fly-in concession camps at peak season

These Etosha vs Okavango figures are our estimates per person per day, sharing, excluding international flights, and they move with the season and the camp. Our Botswana vs Namibia comparison looks at the price gap between the two countries in more detail.

How Do You Get There, and Can You Combine Them?

Etosha is reached by road from Windhoek in around five to six hours, and the Okavango Delta through Maun, from where light aircraft fly into the camps. An Etosha vs Okavango combination takes about 10 to 14 days, either by flying or by driving through Namibia's Zambezi region.

Photo by Rod Long on Unsplash

By road, Halali in the middle of Etosha is about 451 km from Windhoek and Namutoni in the east about 486 km. From Etosha, the drive north-east to the Okavango River near Rundu is roughly 430 km, then about 200 km more to Divundu, where you can cross into Botswana at Mohembo and drive down the Okavango Panhandle towards Maun. Allow two or three days with overnight stops along the river.

Flying is faster: travellers usually return to Windhoek and connect to Maun, or start in Botswana and finish in Namibia. Divulge's 7-day classic Etosha National Park safari pairs well with a short 3-day Okavango Delta mokoro tour for a first taste of both.

Etosha vs Okavango: Which Should You Choose?

For the Etosha vs Okavango choice, pick Etosha if you want reliable sightings at a fair price and like the freedom of a road trip, and the Okavango if you want a quieter, more varied wilderness and can stretch the budget. If you have two weeks and the funds, doing both is the best answer of all.

Choose Etosha if you...

Want to self-drive or travel with children, are on a mid-range budget, hope to see black rhino, or plan to add Namibia's desert and coast.

Choose the Okavango Delta if you...

Want water activities and walking, value privacy over price, hope to see wild dog, or are adding Chobe or Victoria Falls. Our Botswana safari packages show how the Delta links with the rest of the north.

Insider Tips

  • Book the Delta first: On a combined Etosha vs Okavango trip, peak-season Delta camps fill first; fix those dates, then build Etosha around them
  • Ask about water levels: Check whether your Delta camp is a water, land or mixed camp in your month, so mokoro trips are possible
  • Split your Etosha nights: Stay in both the west (Okaukuejo) and the east (Namutoni) to avoid long return drives
  • Use the floodlit waterholes: Sit up after dinner at least one night; rhino sightings often come after dark
  • Pack soft: Light aircraft into the Delta need soft bags within the airline limits
  • Pack warm layers: June to August mornings are cold in both places, especially on open vehicles and boats

Frequently Asked Questions

Etosha vs Okavango: which is better for a first safari?

For most first safaris, Etosha is the easier start: sightings at the waterholes are predictable, roads are good and costs are lower. The Okavango Delta is the richer experience, with water activities, walking and all of the Big Five, but it costs more. In the Etosha vs Okavango choice, first-timers on a moderate budget usually start with Etosha.

Can you see the Big Five in Etosha and the Okavango?

Etosha has elephant, lion, leopard and black rhino but no buffalo, so it cannot offer the full Big Five. The Okavango Delta has all five, although rhino are rare after reintroduction and should be treated as a bonus. Buffalo, elephant, lion and leopard are seen regularly in the Delta in the dry season.

How far is Etosha from the Okavango Delta?

Etosha and the Okavango Delta are a long drive apart. From Etosha it is roughly 430 km to the Okavango River near Rundu and about 200 km more to Divundu, before crossing into Botswana at Mohembo and driving on towards Maun. Most travellers allow two or three days by road, or fly via Windhoek.

What is the best month to visit both Etosha and the Okavango?

The best months to visit both Etosha and the Okavango are July to September. Etosha is dry and animals gather at the waterholes, while the Okavango flood is still high enough for mokoro trips and the game viewing is excellent. August is a strong all-round choice, but it is also the busiest and most expensive time to book.

How many days do you need for Etosha and the Okavango Delta?

Plan at least 10 days for an Etosha vs Okavango trip, and 12 to 14 days if you drive between them. That allows three or four nights in Etosha, two travel days, and three or four nights in the Delta. With less time, choose one and give it the full nights it deserves.

Final Thoughts

The Etosha vs Okavango decision rests on budget and style: Etosha delivers dependable waterhole sightings at a fair price, and the Okavango delivers a quieter, water-based wilderness at a premium. In the dry months from June to October, both are at their best and they combine well in one trip.
